Federal officers may use deadly force but must try to avoid such situations, policy says
While federal officers are permitted to use deadly force to stop an imminent threat of death or serious physical injury, the Department of Homeland Security also tells its officers to remain tactically sound, including avoiding “intentionally and unreasonably placing themselves in positions in which they have no alternative to using deadly force.”
“DHS LEOs (law enforcement officers) should seek to employ tactics and techniques that effectively bring an incident under control while promoting the safety of LEOs and the public, and that minimize the risk of unintended injury or serious property damage,” US Customs and Border Protection policy says.
DHS officers are permitted to use force that is “reasonable in light of the totality of the circumstances,” the policy says. They are not required to wait for an attack before using “reasonable force” to stop a threat.
Gunshots from Monday's shooting in Maine heard in surveillance video
Laura Peters heard gunshots come from the intersection of Pool Street and Hill Street in Biddeford, Maine, around 7:17 a.m. Monday, the Biddeford resident told CNN.
At least four gunshots can be heard in surveillance video captured by Peters’ doorbell camera.
One person was killed Monday in an ICE-involved shooting in Biddeford, according to Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau.
Authorities have not publicly confirmed the person’s identity. CNN has reached out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
Evidence in Alex Pretti, Renee Good killings turned over to state authorities
Hard drives of evidence in a string of Minneapolis shootings earlier this year, previously withheld by the federal government, have been turned over to state authorities, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced Monday.
The evidence trove includes statements and body camera footage in the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, she said. Good and Sosa-Celis were shot by an ICE agent and Pretti was shot by a Border Patrol agent.
Physical evidence, including Good’s SUV, was also delivered to the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, Moriarty said.
“The wonderful thing is now we have all the evidence. We don’t have to speculate about what we don’t have,” Moriarty said.
The handover comes after months of back-and-forth between state and federal authorities over access that drove the state of Minnesota to file a lawsuit against the federal government.
Moriarty said she could not speak as to why federal agencies decided to change course in the investigation.
State investigators will now comb through what Moriarty called a “voluminous” amount of evidence and make a decision on whether or not to file charges against the federal agents.
26-year-old Colombian man killed in Maine ICE shooting, immigrants' rights group says
A 26-year-old Colombian man was killed in the shooting involving ICE officers in Biddeford, Maine, on Monday, according to the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.
Authorities have not publicly confirmed the man’s identity. CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
The young man was authorized to work in the US and was issued a social security number, the group said in a statement. Federal officials have not confirmed those details.
The 26-year-old was headed to work when the shooting occurred, Mufalo Chitam, the group’s executive director, told CNN.
US Sen. Angus King described the individual as a “male in his 20s” who had been ordered removed from the United States.
King said this afternoon the man was not the target of an arrest warrant, reversing his earlier statement after speaking again with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

DHS officials concerned about high-profile ICE incidents
The recent pair of fatal shootings involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — last week in Houston and Monday in Maine — may represent the most serious challenge for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin since he assumed control of the Department of Homeland Security in March.
Mullin was propelled to the role partly as a result of how his predecessor, Kristi Noem, handled a pair of shootings in Minneapolis earlier this year that resulted in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Within the Department of Homeland Security, officials have privately shared concerns repeat instances of ICE-involved shootings will derail public sentiment about the agency, as Mullin has tried to rebuild on the heels of Noem’s ouster, according to a DHS official.
During his confirmation hearing, Mullin said one of his top goals was ensuring ICE would not be in the headlines nearly every day as it had been under his predecessor. He has publicly favored a low-key style of immigration enforcement that relies more on targeted operations rather than the large-scale and largely unfocused sweeps that were a hallmark of Noem’s tenure.
But those targeted operations are now made more difficult by the proliferation of know-your-rights trainings that have popped up in immigrant communities across the country throughout President Donald Trump’s second term. The trainings have encouraged immigrants to not open their doors to immigration authorities, making detaining immigrants at their homes more challenging.
As a result, immigration officers have begun relying more frequently on vehicle stops to apprehend undocumented immigrants. Such was the case in Houston, where Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, was driving a van shortly before he was fatally shot by an ICE agent.

sources.news_title: ICE Involved in Maine shooting, official says
sources.text:
A second fatal shooting linked to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in under a week was reported in Maine on Monday, coming five days after the death of a Mexican national in Texas.
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot and killed while he was on his way to work in Houston, Texas, July 7. ICE said he had "weaponized his vehicle", leading to an officer firing his weapon. No body-cam footage was available for either incident.
On Monday, in Biddeford, Maine, another man was fatally shot by a federal agent.
Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, a Biddeford resident, initially said in a statement shared on Facebook that a shooting occurred in the city and that one person was killed. He said ICE was involved and that the Maine State Police and the Department of Public Safety were responding to gather additional details.
"Our community is shaken by this incident. We are heartbroken that someone lost their life. We deserve answers about why lethal force was used and why an operation was being carried out in our streets," Fecteau said in a later press release shared with Newsweek.
Biddeford ICE Shooting: What We Know
Authorities have not yet released additional information about the circumstances of the shooting, including the identity of the person killed, whether any officers discharged their weapons, or the nature of ICE’s involvement.
The Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition and Presente! Maine later said in a press release that a 26-year-old Colombian man had died in the incident.
“Our communities are hurting…” said MIRC Executive Director Mufalo Chitam. “Today, a 26-year-old member of our community is dead following an incident involving ICE. We are grieving, we are furious, and we will not allow his death to be treated as routine or inevitable. How much more harm must our communities endure before those with the power to act acknowledge that this has gone too far?”
Maine's Attorney General's Office said that, "initial statements indicate an Enforcement Removal Operations Officer was conducting an enforcement operation related to a final order of removal when the subject attempted to flee in a vehicle in the direction of the officer and was fatally shot."
Maine Senator Angus King later told reporters that he had spoken with Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin about the shooting, with the secretary confirming no body cams were worn by the agents. King said he understood the deceased man had a final order of removal, but later said Mullin had clarified that the deceased man was not the initial target of the operation.
Newsweek has repeatedly contacted the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for comment.
Biddeford police referred Newsweek to ICE officials for details regarding the incident. The FBI confirmed to Newsweek that agents were on the scene, but said it could provide no further information.
Blood on the Victim's Head and Face
Daniel Boucher, 71, of Biddeford, said he heard what sounded like firecrackers outside his apartment at about 7:30 am, and ran upstairs to investigate. Federal agents had pulled a young man out of a vehicle as he claimed he was trying to stop. The man then appeared to die at the scene as officers performed CPR, Boucher recalled.
One officer who was being consoled by a colleague said the victim had tried to run him over or ram his vehicle, Boucher said.
"And that was it, that was all I saw,” Boucher told Newsweek. "That was enough to see, actually."
Boucher did not witness any shots fired, but recalled hearing several rounds go off outside of his window early Monday.
"I could see what was happening after the shooting occurred," he said. "I saw [federal agents] trying to ram the vehicle to make him stop. The small white vehicle backed up and proceeded down the street toward me, and then they rammed him again, causing the vehicle to turn and head north on Hill Street. And that's when they pulled him out after that."
Boucher said he saw blood on the victim's head and face.
"Traumatic experience, very traumatizing," he said. "It was a really tough thing to see and hear. It's devastating. It's something you don't think will happen in your community, but then again, why wouldn't it if they keep pursuing the same goals?"
Hill Street and Pool Street in Biddeford were closed Monday morning following the shooting, according to a dispatcher reviewed by TV station NEWS CENTER Maine.
Troy Jackson, a Democratic candidate seeking to replace Graham Platner as the Senate nominee in Maine, said in a post on X that he had been alerted to the fatal ICE shooting in Biddeford and that his team was monitoring the situation. "My heart is with Biddeford – and with all Mainers," Jackson wrote.
Calls For An Independent Investigation
In a statement published on social media, immigrant advocacy collective Project Relief expressed heartbreak over the death of the unnamed individual, whom they described as a young person whose life was cut short.
"We are in contact with the family and are committed to supporting them during this unimaginable time," the organization wrote. "Our community must come together to stand with their loved ones and ensure they are not alone. They must get justice."
Hannah Pingree, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in an online comment that a "life was lost in Biddeford this morning in a shooting involving ICE. I'm monitoring closely and will share updates as they come. Every Mainer deserves safety and security in their own community, along with transparency and a thorough, independent investigation into what happened."
Maine Governor Janet Mills said she had been briefed on the shooting. In a statement shared on X, Mills said, “I know that situations like these are alarming and frightening.”
She said the Maine State Police were at the scene “supporting and working cooperatively with the Attorney General's Office, Maine's Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and Federal officials to determine the facts of what occurred this morning.”
U.S. Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, said on X, "The shooting in Biddeford requires a full and impartial investigation of what happened. It is my understanding that the Biddeford police have secured the site and that the FBI is investigating."
Protests broke out in the city, with some locals visiting Collins' Biddeford office holding signs and demanding action. The GOP Senator has backed recent waves of funding for immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump.
In a statement to Newsweek Monday afternoon, the office of Maine State Attorney General, Aaron M. Frey, said that the agent involved had been placed on leave, and that local officials would be involved with the investigation into the incident.
Video Footage Appears to Show Aftermath of the Shooting
A video circulating on Reddit appeared to show the aftermath of the Biddeford incident showed a white sedan stopped at an intersection near a Hill Street sign, surrounded by multiple law enforcement vehicles with emergency lights activated.
Several officers could be seen gathered around a person lying on the pavement beside the vehicle. Officers appeared to be providing medical assistance, with a medical bag or equipment visible on the ground nearby.
Some individuals in the footage appeared to be wearing tactical vests marked “Police” and “U.S. Marshal,” though the identities and affiliations of those officers could not be independently verified. The video did not independently establish the circumstances leading up to the incident or identify which agencies were involved.
Additional footage from the same scene showed ICE officers operating near a white pickup truck parked along a residential driveway while emergency sirens wailed in the background.
A Growing List of Fatal ICE Shootings
Fatal federal agent-involved shootings have been reported at least nine times during the second Trump administration. The killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti remain the highest-profile incidents, with Good being killed by an ICE officer, and Pretti being shot and killed by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.
In Minnesota on Monday, local officials announced they had received evidence from the federal government related to Good and Pretti's deaths, including statements, bodycam footage, and other evidence linked to the killings. Good's car was also handed to state investigators.
“The wonderful thing now is we have all the evidence,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at a press conference. “Any time the government is responsible in whatever way of taking the life of a community member we need to have a full and thorough investigation.”
Another U.S. citizen, Ruben Ray Martinez, was also fatally shot by an ICE agent in Texas in March 2025, but the connection went unreported until a Newsweek analysis of Freedom of Information Request Act (FOIA) records obtained by American Oversight in February 2026.
In the cases involving Good and Martinez, DHS alleged they had tried to run over federal agents, although video footage left those accounts up for debate.
In Houston, Texas, on July 7, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was also shot by an ICE agent, after he allegedly "weaponized his vehicle," per ICE's account of the incident. The Mexican national had lived in the U.S. for 35 years and had three American citizen sons.
Officials in Houston also promised a thorough, independent investigation into the events surrounding Salgado Araujo's death.
Have you witnessed the incident in Biddeford or captured video, photos, or other footage? If you have information, please contact b.rahman@newsweek.com.

Earlier this year, Maine became the latest state to see a surge in ICE agents as part of the Trump administration’s Operation Catch of the Day. That surge was cut short amid a nationwide pushback against the agency’s tactics following the fatal shootings of two protesters in Minneapolis.

One killed in encounter with ICE agents in Maine
BIDDEFORD, Maine – A person was fatally shot on Monday during an encounter with U.S. immigration agents in Maine, a top state lawmaker said, days after a man was killed by a U.S. agent during a traffic stop in Texas.
“This morning a shooting occurred in Biddeford. A person was killed. ICE was involved,” Ryan Fecteau, the Democratic speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and a native of Biddeford, wrote on Facebook.
Details remained unclear, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Department of Homeland Security officials could not be reached for comment. The FBI said it responded immediately to assist at the scene of the shooting but did not offer any additional information. The Biddeford police did not comment and referred questions to ICE.
Immigration advocates said the person shot was a 26-year-old Colombian man who was authorized to work in the U.S. and had a Social Security number, though they did not name him or say how they were able to identify him.
“This is devastating, enraging, and unacceptable,” the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition and Presente! Maine said in a statement. “His loved ones deserve answers, and the public deserves a full and transparent account of what happened.”
U.S. Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, told reporters that he had spoken with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and that the person killed was a man in his 20s. King also said that the agents were apparently not wearing body cameras.
“What I said to the secretary was, we want a full, transparent and open investigation of this matter,” he said.
One eyewitness, Daniel Boucher, 71, a caregiver and part-time drafter who lives in downtown Biddeford, said in an interview that he was on the second floor of his apartment when he heard what sounded like firecrackers around 7:30 a.m.
He ran to the window and saw a white SUV ram a smaller white car more than once, causing the car to change direction. At that point, Boucher said, he saw an ICE officer get out of the SUV and try to open the other car’s door before pulling a man out.
The man, whom Boucher described as looking like a younger man, had blood on his face and his head, and the officer put him on the ground.
“Initially I remember hearing the victim say, ‘But I tried to stop,’” Boucher said.
An officer who appeared to be the one who shot the man looked “very distraught, almost in shock,” according to Boucher, and said that the victim had tried to ram him or hit him.
Eventually, Boucher said, the wounded man appeared to stop breathing.
“I’ll be very honest with you, I am not pro-ICE at all,” he said. “And I am a Democrat. But regardless of that, what I’m telling you is what I experienced today.”
Some videos surrounding the incident also began to emerge on Monday, including one posted on social media and verified by Reuters that showed a white car driving in what appeared to be an aimless circle, with two men wearing vests on foot trying to stop it. Photos taken at the scene showed the car with what looked like bullet holes in the windshield, stopped against the side of a large white SUV with emergency lights flashing.
PROTESTS BREAK OUT
The shooting prompted protests in Biddeford, a city of over 21,000 people 15 miles south of Portland.
About 200 demonstrators gathered at a park, holding signs and chanting, before marching about a quarter mile up the road to the Biddeford office of Republican U.S. Senator Susan Collins, who is running for reelection this year.
Ten protesters entered the building’s foyer, chanting “ICE out!” and “Vote her out!” and screaming obscenities. A representative from Collins’ office came out and tried to talk to some of them. There were no arrests or violence.
Six days ago, an ICE agent fatally shot a man identified as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston during a traffic stop, sparking protests in the city’s heavily Hispanic East End.

Three men who witnessed the shooting have challenged ICE’s account, a lawyer for two of the men told reporters on Friday. Salgado, a father of three, was a construction worker in the process of obtaining a work permit, relatives have said.
The shootings took place amid a nationwide surge in arrests of immigrants as part of President Donald Trump’s federal crackdown on migrants that has drawn objections from local Democratic leaders and protests in multiple cities.

Since the beginning of June, ICE arrests in Maine have more than quadrupled to around 70 per day in early July, according to internal ICE data shared with Reuters by a source.
